words: question; answer; detail; the text says; page; line; reread
notes: Ask and answer questions about a story or an article and point to the exact words that answer them: the student says or writes where in the text the answer is (page, paragraph, line) and rereads to check. RL.3.1 and RI.3.1 are the same skill on literature and on information, so they share a row; every unit practises it on its anchor texts, from short stories and articles of 300 to 800 words in unit 1 to chapters of the unit 3 chapter book. Grade 2 asked who, what, where, when, why and how questions about key details; grade 3 adds referring explicitly to the text as the basis for the answer, so an answer with no place in the text is not yet an answer. Limit: answers stay with what the text states or plainly shows; inference that the student must explain is grade 4 (RL.4.1).

words: fable; folktale; myth; moral; lesson; central message; recount; key detail
cross_subject: social-studies:ss2-culture-migration (stories carried by families from many places)
notes: Recount a fable, folktale or myth in order (who, problem, events, end) and state its central message, lesson or moral, then show which key details carry it. Practised on short traditional tales from many cultures and on the unit 2 explanatory tales (why the frog has a long tongue: original tales in the style of a pourquoi tale), 300 to 900 words, read aloud first then read closely. Grade 2 recounted fables and folktales and named the message; grade 3 adds myths and asks the student to explain how the message is conveyed through key details. Limit: a message, lesson or moral, stated plainly; theme as a reading of a whole text built from details is grade 4 (RL.4.2). Folktales and myths come from named cultures and peoples, with a note on where each was told.

words: character; trait; motivation; feeling; action; event; because; so
notes: Describe a character by traits, motivations and feelings, using what the character says and does, and explain how the character's actions cause the next events. Practised on unit 1 stories of children who work to learn to read and go to school, and on the unit 3 chapter book read whole (about 10,000 to 20,000 words across the unit). Grade 2 described how characters respond to major events; grade 3 turns the arrow round: the character's actions drive the sequence of events. A trait word is always tied to an action in the text. Limit: one character at a time; describing in depth with thoughts, words and actions is grade 4, comparing two characters grade 5. Teacher note: some unit 1 stories show children kept from school by war or poverty; the teacher previews them and frames them through the children's determination, not the danger.

words: literal; nonliteral; phrase; expression; meaning; shades of meaning; suspected; wondered
notes: Work out what words and phrases mean as they are used in a story or poem, and tell literal from nonliteral language (take steps, a heart of gold). RL.3.4 gives the reading task; L.3.5 adds the word work: literal and nonliteral meanings in context (5a), real-life connections between words and their use (5b), and shades of meaning among words for states of mind and certainty, knew, believed, suspected, heard, wondered (5c). Practised on the unit 2 frog poems and the unit 3 chapter book. Grade 2 looked at how rhythm, rhyme and repeated lines supply meaning; grade 3 is the first year to separate literal from nonliteral meaning, so it introduces the figurative-language model. Limit: nonliteral phrases are named and explained; simile, metaphor, idiom and proverb as named kinds are grade 4 (L.4.5).

words: chapter; scene; stanza; verse; part; builds on; earlier; later
notes: Use the words chapter, scene and stanza when talking or writing about a text, and describe how each part builds on the parts before it (what chapter 4 adds to what chapter 3 set up). Practised mostly on the unit 3 chapter book read whole, with a short play scene and stanzas of the unit 2 poems. Grade 2 described a story's overall structure, the beginning that introduces and the ending that concludes; grade 3 follows a longer text part by part, so it introduces the narrative-arc model (setup, rising problem, turning point, resolution) on top of grade 2's story map. Limit: naming parts and saying how each builds; the structural elements of poems and drama by name are grade 4 (RL.4.5), and how all the parts fit one structure is grade 5 (RL.5.5).

words: point of view; narrator; character; author; I think; the author thinks; agree; disagree
cross_subject: social-studies:ss2-two-accounts (two people can tell the same event differently)
notes: Tell one's own point of view apart from the narrator's or a character's (RL.3.6) and from the author's in an article (RI.3.6): what does the character think, what does the author think, what do I think, and how do I know each from the text. The same skill on two kinds of text, so one row. Practised on the unit 3 chapter book (do you agree with what the main character decides) and the unit 4 water articles (what the author wants readers to believe about water use). Grade 2 acknowledged differences among characters' points of view and named an author's purpose; grade 3 adds the reader's own view as a third voice and keeps the three apart. Limit: distinguishing views; first and third person narration is grade 4.

words: illustration; photograph; map; caption; mood; setting; where; when; how
cross_subject: social-studies:ss3-map-skills (reading a map with title, key and scale)
notes: Explain what pictures add to words. In stories (RL.3.7): how an illustration creates mood or stresses part of a character or setting. In information (RI.3.7): use maps, photographs and diagrams with the words to show where, when, why and how events happen. The two codes are one skill on two kinds of text. Practised on the unit 1 picture books (where the children in the stories live, on a world map) and the unit 2 frog texts (diagrams of a life cycle, photographs of frogs in their habitats). Grade 2 used pictures to understand characters, setting and plot and explained how a diagram clarifies a text; grade 3 asks how the picture contributes something the words do not. Limit: still images in one text; charts, graphs and timelines are grade 4 (RI.4.7).

words: series; author; same characters; theme; setting; plot; compare; contrast; alike; different
notes: Compare and contrast the themes, settings and plots of two stories by the same author about the same characters. Practised on the unit 3 set: two books of one original Curio Class chapter-book series, the first read whole as a class and the second read in part or as the independent book (see For the lead). Grade 2 compared versions of the same story by different authors or cultures; grade 3 holds the author and characters fixed and compares what changes from book to book. Students use a two-column story map for each book, then a sentence frame for alike and different. Limit: one author, one series; comparing how stories from different cultures treat a theme is grade 4 (RL.4.9).

words: chapter book; article; independent reading; reading log; stamina; band
notes: Read stories, plays, poems and information texts at the high end of the grades 2 to 3 complexity band (measure about 420 to 820 in the 2012 supplement's table) on one's own by the end of the year, with help fading across the four units. RL.3.10 and RI.3.10 are the same demand on the two kinds of text. Practised through the year's anchors (about half literary, half informational) plus a daily independent reading block with a log and a teacher conference, including one chapter book read whole in unit 3. Grade 2 read in the same band with scaffolding at the high end; grade 3 reads the high end independently and proficiently, the first year the band's top is reached alone. Limit: proficiency in the 2 to 3 band; the 4 to 5 band begins in grade 4.

words: main idea; key detail; support; topic; paragraph; recount
cross_subject: science:3-LS1-1 (the main idea of a life-cycle text)
notes: State the main idea of an article or chapter, recount its key details and explain how each supports the main idea (RI.3.2). SL.3.2 does the same for a text read aloud or information in a video, chart or talk. Practised on unit 1 true accounts of people who bring books to children, and unit 2 frog articles of 400 to 900 words with headings. Grade 2 identified the main topic and the focus of paragraphs; grade 3 moves from topic (what it is about) to main idea (what it says about it) and makes the student justify each detail's place. Limit: one main idea per text or section; two or more main ideas is grade 5, a written summary grade 4.

words: sequence; first; next; then; cause; effect; because; as a result; compare; connection
cross_subject: science:3-LS1-1 (stages of a life cycle in order)
notes: Describe how events, ideas or steps in an information text connect, using words of time, sequence and cause and effect (RI.3.3), and describe the logical link between sentences and paragraphs: comparison, cause and effect, first, second, third (RI.3.8). Together they introduce the text-structure model: the student names the link and finds the signal words. Practised on the unit 2 frog texts (a frog's life cycle in order; why a frog's skin or colour helps it live) and unit 4 water texts (what happens when a well is dug). Grade 2 described the connection between events or steps and how reasons support an author's points; grade 3 adds the language of time, sequence and cause, and looks at how sentences and paragraphs link. Limit: links within one text; naming the overall structure of a whole text is grade 4 (RI.4.5).

words: heading; sidebar; caption; key word; search; hyperlink; index; glossary; locate
notes: Use text features and search tools (key words, sidebars, hyperlinks, headings, index) to find information on a given topic quickly. Practised in unit 2, where students find answers to their own questions about frogs in print books and on a small set of chosen web pages, and again in unit 4 research on water. Grade 2 used captions, bold print, subheadings, glossaries and indexes to find key facts; grade 3 adds sidebars, key word searches and hyperlinks and asks for information relevant to a topic, not just a fact. Limit: on a given topic with chosen sources; locating answers across several print and digital sources is grade 5 (RI.5.7). Teacher note: web searching is done on a teacher-chosen list of pages.

words: compare; contrast; both; only; important point; same topic
cross_subject: science:2-ESS2-3 (where water is found on Earth)
notes: Compare and contrast the most important points and key details of two texts on the same topic. Practised in unit 4 on two water texts (one on how far people walk for water, one on how a town cleans its water), and in unit 2 on two frog texts. Grade 2 compared the most important points of two texts; grade 3 adds the key details and expects a table or Venn chart of points both make and points only one makes. Limit: two texts, side by side; joining two texts into one piece of writing or speaking is grade 4 (RI.4.9).

words: habitat; adaptation; predator; life cycle; freshwater; pollution; conserve; after; during
cross_subject: science:3-LS4-3 (words for habitat and survival)
notes: Learn and use the general academic and domain words of the grade 3 topics. RI.3.4 is working out their meaning in a text on a grade 3 topic; L.3.6 is using them accurately in talk and writing, including words for space and time (after dinner that night, beneath, during). Each unit has one word list from its texts, mostly general academic words, met before, during and after reading and returning in later units. Grade 2 learned words in a text on a grade 2 topic and used words acquired from reading; grade 3 names general academic and domain words as two kinds and adds the spatial and temporal words. Limit: the grade 3 topics; words for precise actions and emotions are grade 4 (L.4.6).

words: context; clue; prefix; suffix; root; glossary; dictionary; meaning
notes: Work out an unknown or multiple-meaning word with a strategy chosen for it: sentence context (4a), a known affix added to a known word, agreeable and disagreeable, care and careless (4b), a known root (company, companion, 4c), a glossary or beginning dictionary in print or online (4d). Practised on words the unit texts supply, never on lists cut from a text. Grade 2 used prefixes only and predicted compound words; grade 3 adds suffixes, choosing flexibly among strategies, and using the dictionary for the precise meaning. Limit: known English affixes and roots; Greek and Latin roots are grade 4 (L.4.4b). The reading of the same word parts is taught on e3-long-words.

words: syllable; prefix; suffix; base word; vowel team; closed; open; irregular; decode
notes: A taught sequence for reading long words: the six syllable types reviewed, then dividing two- and three-syllable words, the common prefixes (un-, re-, dis-, pre-, mis-) and derivational suffixes (-ful, -less, -ness, -ly, -able) with their meanings (3a), common Latin suffixes (-tion, -sion, -ment, -ous) (3b), multisyllable words (3c) and the year's irregular words (3d). Short daily lessons with word lists, then sentences and passages using the pattern, and a check every few weeks with next steps. Grade 2 decoded two-syllable words with long vowels and words with common prefixes and suffixes; grade 3 moves to any multisyllable word and to meaning-bearing parts. The rule of the approach: words are read, never guessed from a picture or the sentence. Limit: grade 3 patterns; combined morphology in unfamiliar words is grade 4.

words: fluency; accuracy; rate; expression; phrasing; reread; self-correct; recording
notes: Read grade-level prose and poetry aloud with accuracy, a natural rate and expression on repeated readings (4b), read with purpose and understanding (4a), and use context to confirm or fix a misread word, rereading as needed (4c). SL.3.5 is the product: an audio recording of a story or poem read fluently, with a picture or display where it helps. Practised on a short passage of each anchor (100 to 250 words) reread with a partner, and on poems in unit 2. Grade 2 asked the same with plain text; grade 3 adds poetry and the recording made for listeners. A one-minute oral reading check (teacher holds the watch, no timer shown to the student) is given three times a year. Limit: context is used to confirm a word already read, never to replace reading it.

words: opinion; reason; because; therefore; since; for example; conclusion; recommend
cross_subject: social-studies:ss3-claim-evidence (a claim backed by reasons)
notes: Write an opinion piece on a topic or text: introduce it, state the opinion, give reasons in an organized list, link them with because, therefore, since, for example, and end with a concluding statement (1a to 1d). Practised on a review of the unit 3 chapter book (would you recommend it to a friend, and why) and a unit 4 opinion essay on why saving water matters, drawing reasons from the texts. Grade 2 named an opinion with reasons and simple linking words (because, and, also); grade 3 adds an organizational structure that lists reasons and more linking words. Limit: reasons are given; reasons backed by facts and details are grade 4 (W.4.1). Model piece and rubric for the opinion type, used all year.

words: topic; fact; definition; detail; also; another; group; conclusion
cross_subject: science:3-LS4-2 (explaining how a trait helps an animal survive)
notes: Write informative text that introduces a topic, groups related information (with pictures where they help), develops it with facts, definitions and details, links ideas with also, another, and, more, but, and ends with a concluding statement (2a to 2d). Practised on unit 1 paragraphs on why getting books is hard in some places, unit 2 paragraphs and a short essay on one frog's adaptations from research, and a unit 4 letter. Grade 2 introduced a topic and used facts and definitions; grade 3 adds grouping related information and linking words within a group. Writing builds from one paragraph to three linked paragraphs by the end of unit 2. Limit: grouping in paragraphs; sections with headings and quotations are grade 4.

words: narrator; character; dialogue; event; first; after that; finally; closure; describe
notes: Write a narrative that sets up a situation and a narrator or characters, unfolds events in a natural order, uses dialogue and descriptions of actions, thoughts and feelings, signals order with time words, and closes (3a to 3d). L.3.3 adds choosing words and phrases for effect (3a), taught as the revising step of the narrative; its second part, spoken and written English (3b), is taught on e3-speaking-reports. Practised on an explanatory tale about a frog (unit 2, after reading such tales) and a rewritten scene from the unit 3 chapter book. Grade 2 recounted a short sequence with details and time words; grade 3 adds a narrator, dialogue and an event sequence that unfolds naturally. Limit: dialogue and description; pacing and sensory detail as named techniques are grade 4 and 5.

words: task; purpose; plan; short write; draft; on demand; notebook
notes: Produce writing whose development and organization fit the task and purpose, with adult guidance (W.3.4), and write routinely: daily short responses to the day's text in one sitting, and longer pieces over days with research and revision (W.3.10). Practised every reading day: the exit question is a written answer that needs the day's text. Over the year, about 30 percent opinion, 35 informative and 35 narrative (the rubric's grades 3 to 5 shares). Grade 3 is the first year these two standards apply. Limit: with guidance and support from adults; grade 4 adds the audience and drops the guidance clause. W.3.9 (drawing evidence) does not exist in grade 3; text-based answers here practise RL.3.1 and RI.3.1.

words: plan; draft; revise; edit; feedback; publish; type; keyboard
notes: Plan, draft, revise and edit with guidance from peers and adults (W.3.5), and use technology to produce and publish writing, with keyboarding, and to work with others (W.3.6). Each unit takes at least one piece through the whole process, with a model piece, a named feedback step (peer critique against one look-for, then teacher feedback) and a published product: the unit 1 strategy bookmark, the unit 2 frog book page, the unit 4 water announcement. Grade 2 revised and edited with guidance and used digital tools; grade 3 makes planning a taught step and begins keyboarding. Editing checks the grade 3 language rows. Limit: no page count for typing yet (grade 4: one page in a sitting). Teacher note: a room without devices handwrites and publishes on paper; keyboarding practice then moves to the home or library session.

words: research; question; source; notes; category; expert; fact; gather
cross_subject: science:3-LS4-2 (researching frog traits that help survival)
notes: Carry out short research projects that build knowledge about a topic (W.3.7): ask a question, read sources chosen by the teacher, take brief notes, sort them into given categories (W.3.8), then write and share. Practised in unit 2 (expert groups each research one unusual frog and its adaptations, notes sorted under body, habitat, how it survives) and unit 4 (one water problem). Grade 2 did shared research as a class and gathered information from given sources to answer a question; grade 3 has students take their own brief notes and sort them. Limit: provided sources and provided categories; categorising on one's own and listing sources is grade 4 (W.4.8).

words: discuss; prepare; agree; build on; ask; explain; evidence; on topic
notes: Take part in discussions in pairs, groups and with the teacher, prepared by having read the text (1a), following agreed norms (1b), asking questions to check understanding and linking to others' comments (1c), and explaining one's own ideas in light of the discussion (1d). SL.3.3 adds asking and answering questions about what a speaker said, with detail. A taught discussion routine with roles, sentence frames that fade, and two or three planned text questions; a formal text-based discussion at least twice a unit, partner talk daily. Grade 2 followed rules and built on others' talk; grade 3 adds coming prepared and explaining one's ideas after hearing others. Limit: assigned roles and reviewing key ideas are grade 4.

words: report; recount; complete sentence; clear; pace; audience; spoken; written
notes: Report on a topic or text, tell a story or recount an experience with facts and descriptive details, speaking clearly at an understandable pace (SL.3.4), in complete sentences when the task calls for detail (SL.3.6). L.3.3b adds noticing how spoken and written English differ (what a talk can do that a page cannot, and the reverse); L.3.3 itself sits on e3-narrative. Practised on the unit 4 water announcement and on short reports from the unit 2 research. Grade 2 told a story audibly in coherent sentences; grade 3 adds a report on a topic or text with facts and a pace an audience can follow. Limit: organizing a report around a main idea is grade 4 (SL.4.4).

words: plural; noun; abstract noun; verb; past; present; future; comparative; superlative
notes: The word-form parts of L.3.1, taught on sentences from the anchor texts and students' own drafts: regular and irregular plurals (1b), abstract nouns such as childhood and freedom (1c), regular and irregular verbs (1d), simple past, present and future tenses (1e), comparative and superlative adjectives and adverbs and choosing between them (1g). Short openers, then use in the week's writing and in editing. Grade 2 used collective nouns, frequent irregular plurals and irregular past verbs; grade 3 completes the regular and irregular patterns and adds tense and comparison. Limit: simple tenses; progressive is grade 4, perfect grade 5. The parent L.3.1 is owned on e3-sentences.

words: noun; pronoun; verb; adjective; adverb; and; but; because; when; simple; compound; complex
notes: The sentence parts of L.3.1: explain what nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs do in a particular sentence (1a), make subjects and verbs and pronouns and their nouns agree (1f), use coordinating and subordinating conjunctions (1h), and produce simple, compound and complex sentences (1i). Taught by sentence combining on sentences from the anchor texts: two short sentences joined with and, but, because, when, then the student's own sentence revised the same way. Grade 2 produced, expanded and rearranged simple and compound sentences; grade 3 adds complex sentences with subordinating conjunctions. Owns L.3.1; the word-form parts are on e3-word-forms. Limit: complete sentences are produced; finding and fixing fragments and run-ons is grade 4 (L.4.1f).

words: capital; title; comma; address; quotation marks; dialogue; possessive; spelling pattern; dictionary
notes: Capitalize words in titles (2a), use commas in addresses (2b), commas and quotation marks in dialogue (2c, taught with the narrative), form possessives (2d), spell high-frequency and studied words and words with suffixes (sitting, smiled, cries, happiness, 2e), use spelling patterns and rules (word families, syllable patterns, ending rules, word parts, 2f), and check spellings in a beginning dictionary (2g). Spelling follows the same pattern sequence as e3-long-words, so the words read in the week are the words spelled. Grade 2 capitalized holidays and names, used commas in letters and apostrophes; grade 3 adds dialogue punctuation, possessives and suffix spelling rules. Practised in editing every process piece.

words: detail; example; infer; inference; evidence; explicit; the text suggests
notes: Refer to details and examples in a text when explaining what it says outright and when drawing inferences (RL.4.1 on literature, RI.4.1 on information, one skill). W.4.9 is the same work in writing: drawing evidence from texts to support analysis, reflection and research, applying the grade 4 reading standards to literature (9a) and information (9b). Practised daily on every unit's anchors: the verse novel (unit 1), animal defense articles (unit 2), the history set and play (unit 3) and the chapter book of unit 4. Grade 3 asked and answered questions referring explicitly to the text; grade 4 adds inference and the student must explain how the detail supports it. W.4.9 begins in grade 4. Limit: refer to and paraphrase; quoting accurately is grade 5 (RL.5.1).

words: theme; summary; summarize; detail; message; poem; drama
notes: Determine a theme of a story, drama or poem from its details, and summarize the text. Practised on unit 1 poems and the verse novel read whole (what the boy comes to understand about writing), and on the unit 4 chapter book, chapter by chapter (each chapter's theme with the events that show it). Grade 3 recounted traditional stories and stated a central message; grade 4 reads theme across any story, drama or poem from details and adds a written summary (who, what, how it ends, in order, without opinion). Limit: one theme, supported; how characters' responses to challenges or a speaker's reflection build the theme is grade 5 (RL.5.2).

words: character; setting; event; thoughts; words; actions; describe in depth; change
notes: Describe in depth a character, setting or event, drawing on specific details: what the character thinks, says and does, what the setting shows, what an event changes. Practised on the unit 1 verse novel (how the main character changes across the year), the unit 3 play (a family member choosing a side) and the unit 4 chapter book. Grade 3 described a character's traits, motives and feelings and how actions drive events; grade 4 adds settings and events as subjects and asks for depth: several specific details joined into one description. Limit: one character, setting or event; comparing two is grade 5 (RL.5.3).

words: simile; metaphor; idiom; adage; proverb; synonym; antonym; allusion; myth
notes: Work out what words and phrases mean in a literary text, including words that allude to characters from myths (Herculean, a quest, an Achilles' heel) (RL.4.4). L.4.5 adds figurative language and word relations: simple similes and metaphors explained in context (5a), common idioms, adages and proverbs (5b), and words related to their antonyms and to near-synonyms (5c). Practised on the unit 1 poems (simile and metaphor in short free verse and rhymed poems) and the unit 4 chapter book (idioms in dialogue), with short myths read for the allusions. Grade 3 told literal from nonliteral meaning; grade 4 names the kinds and adds allusion. Limit: simple similes and metaphors are explained; interpreting figurative language in a whole passage is grade 5 (L.5.5a).

words: poem; verse; rhythm; meter; line; drama; cast of characters; stage directions; dialogue; prose; version
notes: Explain the main differences between poems, drama and prose, and use their terms when speaking or writing: verse, rhythm, meter in poems; cast of characters, setting, descriptions, dialogue, stage directions in drama (RL.4.5). RL.4.7 adds comparing a story or play with a visual or oral presentation of it and saying where each version follows the text's descriptions and directions. Practised on the unit 1 poems and verse novel against prose (the same moment told both ways) and the unit 3 short play, read aloud and then watched or performed. Grade 3 named chapters, scenes and stanzas and how parts build; grade 4 explains what makes each form a form. Limit: structural elements named and used; how chapters or scenes fit an overall structure is grade 5.

words: narrator; first person; third person; I; he; she; they; point of view
notes: Compare and contrast the point of view from which different stories are told, including first and third person: who is telling, what that narrator can and cannot know. Practised on the unit 1 verse novel (first person, a boy's poem-journal) against third person stories, and on the unit 3 history set (a first person letter beside a third person story of the same time). Grade 3 told the reader's own view apart from a narrator's or character's; grade 4 compares narrations and names the person. Limit: naming and comparing the narration; how the narrator's view shapes the telling is grade 5 (RL.5.6).

words: myth; legend; traditional tale; culture; quest; good and evil; pattern; theme; compare
cross_subject: social-studies:ss4-regional-cultures (stories of peoples in different regions)
notes: Compare and contrast how stories, myths and traditional tales from different cultures treat similar themes (good against evil, a promise kept) and patterns of events (the quest, the trickster, three trials). Practised on a short set of myths and traditional tales from at least three cultures, 500 to 1,500 words each, read alongside the unit 1 or unit 3 texts (see For the lead for placement), with the narrative arc used to line up their events. Grade 3 compared stories by one author about the same characters; grade 4 crosses cultures and compares patterns. Limit: traditional literature; comparing stories of one modern genre is grade 5 (RL.5.9). Each tale is credited to the people who tell it.

words: chapter book; verse novel; play; article; independent reading; log; band
notes: Read stories, plays, poems and information texts in the grades 4 to 5 complexity band (measure about 740 to 1010 in the 2012 supplement's table) proficiently, with scaffolding at the high end. RL.4.10 and RI.4.10 are one demand on two kinds of text. Practised through the year's anchors (about half literary, half informational), at least two long texts read whole (the unit 1 verse novel and the unit 4 chapter book) and a daily independent reading block with a log and conference. Grade 3 reached the top of the 2 to 3 band on its own; grade 4 enters a new, higher band, so scaffolding returns at its high end. Limit: proficiency with scaffolding; independent at the high end is grade 5.

words: main idea; key detail; summary; summarize; paraphrase; in my own words
cross_subject: science:4-LS1-1 (summarizing how body structures help an animal survive)
notes: Determine the main idea of an information text, explain how key details support it, and write a summary (RI.4.2). SL.4.2 adds paraphrasing part of a text read aloud or information in a video, chart or talk. Practised on the unit 2 animal defense texts (about 600 to 1,200 words, sections with headings) and the unit 3 history articles. Grade 3 stated a main idea and explained how details support it; grade 4 adds a written summary and paraphrase in one's own words. Limit: one main idea per text; two or more is grade 5 (RI.5.2).

words: explain; procedure; concept; what happened; why; because; result
cross_subject: science:4-LS1-1 (how a structure works to protect an animal)
notes: Explain events, procedures, ideas or concepts in a history, science or technical text, including what happened and why, from specific information in the text. Practised on the unit 2 animal defense texts (how a pufferfish's defense works, step by step) and the unit 3 history set (why the people of one place split into sides). Grade 3 described relationships among events, ideas or steps with time and cause words; grade 4 explains them, so the student must give the why from the text. Limit: one event, idea or process; how two or more interact is grade 5 (RI.5.3).

words: structure; chronology; comparison; cause and effect; problem and solution; signal word
cross_subject: science:4-ESS3-2 (problem and solution texts on reducing hazards)
notes: Describe the overall structure of a text or part of a text: chronology, comparison, cause and effect, problem and solution. Practised on the unit 2 and unit 3 information texts, sorted by structure, and used again in writing (the informative essay borrows a structure). Grade 3 described links between particular sentences and paragraphs; grade 4 names the structure of a whole text or section. Limit: one text's structure; comparing the structures of two or more texts is grade 5 (RI.5.5).

words: firsthand account; secondhand account; eyewitness; focus; information; letter; diary
cross_subject: social-studies:ss4-primary-source (what a source made at the time can tell us)
notes: Compare and contrast a firsthand and a secondhand account of the same event or topic, and describe how their focus and information differ. Practised on the unit 4 set (a letter or diary of someone who was there beside a later article about the same event) and the unit 3 history set. Grade 3 told the reader's own view from the author's; grade 4 compares two accounts and asks why they differ (who saw it, when it was written). Limit: one firsthand and one secondhand account; analysing several accounts and the points of view they represent is grade 5 (RI.5.6).

words: chart; graph; diagram; timeline; key; label; data; interpret
cross_subject: math:3.MD.B.3 (reading scaled bar graphs and picture graphs)
notes: Interpret information shown in charts, graphs, diagrams, timelines or interactive parts of web pages, and explain how it adds to understanding the text it sits in. Practised on the unit 2 animal texts (a labelled diagram of a defense, a bar graph of predator numbers) and the unit 3 history set (a timeline of the period). Grade 3 used maps, photographs and illustrations with the words; grade 4 adds quantitative and time displays and asks how each contributes. Limit: displays inside one text; drawing on several print and digital sources to answer a question is grade 5 (RI.5.7). Uses graph reading taught in grade 3 math.

words: point; reason; evidence; support; claim; convince; speaker
cross_subject: social-studies:ss3-claim-evidence (a claim backed by evidence)
notes: Explain how an author uses reasons and evidence to support particular points (RI.4.8), and identify the reasons and evidence a speaker gives (SL.4.3). Introduces the claim-evidence-reasoning model in ELA (point, the reason given for it, the evidence for the reason), the same tool science and social studies use. Practised on the unit 3 history set (a broadside or speech urging people to take a side) and the unit 4 speeches and articles on unfair rules. Grade 3 described the logical link between sentences and paragraphs; grade 4 follows how reasons and evidence hold up a point. Limit: explaining the support; matching which reason supports which point when there are several is grade 5 (RI.5.8).

words: integrate; combine; both texts; source; knowledgeable; topic
notes: Integrate information from two texts on the same topic in order to write or speak about it knowledgeably. Practised in unit 2 (two texts on one animal's defenses joined in an informative essay) and unit 3 (two accounts joined in a discussion). Grade 3 compared the important points and details of two texts side by side; grade 4 joins them into one piece of writing or talk. Limit: two texts; several texts is grade 5 (RI.5.9).

words: predator; prey; venom; camouflage; mimicry; colonist; loyal; protest; stammered; whined
cross_subject: science:4-LS1-1 (words for animal structures and functions)
notes: Learn and use the general academic and domain words of the grade 4 topics: working out their meaning in a text on a grade 4 topic (RI.4.4) and using them accurately (L.4.6), including words for precise actions, emotions and states of being (quizzed, whined, stammered) and words basic to a topic (wildlife, conservation, endangered). One word list per unit from its texts, each word met before, during and after reading and again in a later unit. Grade 3 added spatial and temporal words; grade 4 adds precision in actions and feelings and topic-basic words. Limit: grade 4 topics; words of contrast and addition (however, although) are grade 5.

words: context; definition; example; restatement; root; affix; graph; photo; thesaurus; pronunciation
notes: Choose a strategy for an unknown or multiple-meaning word: context such as a definition, example or restatement in the text (4a), common Greek and Latin affixes and roots (telegraph, photograph, autograph, 4b), and dictionaries, glossaries and thesauruses in print and online for pronunciation and precise meaning (4c). Practised on words the unit texts supply (unit 2 science words carry many Greek and Latin roots). Grade 3 used sentence context, English affixes and known roots; grade 4 names the kinds of context clue, adds Greek and Latin parts and the thesaurus. Limit: common grade 4 roots; context that works through cause and effect or comparison is grade 5 (L.5.4a).

words: syllable; root; prefix; suffix; schwa; stress; base; multisyllabic
notes: A taught sequence for reading unfamiliar multisyllabic words in and out of context, using all letter-sound knowledge, syllable division and morphology together (3a): syllable types in three- and four-syllable words, the schwa and stress shift (nation, national), more prefixes and suffixes, and the first Greek and Latin roots (port, rupt, graph, tele). Short daily lessons on word lists, then the same patterns in sentences and the anchor passages, with a check and next steps every few weeks. Grade 3 decoded multisyllable words and common suffixes and prefixes; grade 4 combines all the parts on unfamiliar words, so the words are longer and less regular. Words are read, never guessed.

words: fluency; accuracy; rate; expression; phrasing; reread; self-correct; performance
notes: Read grade-level prose and poetry aloud with accuracy, a natural rate and expression on successive readings (4b), with purpose and understanding (4a), using context to confirm or fix word recognition (4c). Practised by rereading a short anchor passage with a partner, and above all on the unit 1 poems read aloud for an audience and the unit 3 play read in parts. A one-minute oral reading check three times a year, the teacher holding the watch. Grade 3 and grade 4 share the wording; grade 4's demand rises because the texts are in the grades 4 to 5 band, longer and with more multisyllabic words, and the poems use rhythm and meter. Limit: rereading is for meaning and expression, not speed alone.

words: opinion; reason; fact; detail; for instance; in order to; in addition; conclusion
notes: Write opinion pieces that introduce the topic or text clearly, state the opinion, group related ideas to support it (1a), give reasons supported by facts and details (1b), link opinion and reasons with phrases such as for instance, in order to, in addition (1c), and conclude in a way tied to the opinion (1d). Practised on the unit 3 piece urging people of the time to join one side, written from the history set, and a unit 4 piece on how students can make a difference. Grade 3 gave a list of reasons; grade 4 asks that each reason be backed by facts and details from the texts, the claim-evidence-reasoning model in writing. Limit: reasons in a logical order is grade 5.

words: introduce; paragraph; section; heading; quotation; example; precise; another; for example; conclusion
cross_subject: science:4-LS1-1 (explaining how an animal structure supports survival)
notes: Write informative text that introduces a topic clearly and groups information in paragraphs and sections, with headings, pictures and media where useful (2a), develops it with facts, definitions, concrete details, quotations and examples (2b), links ideas with another, for example, also, because (2c), uses precise and domain words (2d) and concludes (2e). Practised on the unit 1 paragraph on what inspired a poet, the unit 2 multi-paragraph essay on one animal's defenses, and the unit 4 literary essay on a theme. Introduces the essay-structure model (introduction, body paragraphs, conclusion). Grade 3 grouped related information; grade 4 adds sections, quotations and precise words. Limit: a general observation and focus is grade 5.

words: orient; narrator; dialogue; description; transition; sensory detail; concrete; conclusion
notes: Write narratives that orient the reader with a situation and narrator or characters (3a), use dialogue and description (3b), manage the sequence with a variety of transition words (3c), use concrete words and sensory details (3d) and give a conclusion that follows from the events (3e). Practised on a branching adventure story about the unit 2 animal (facts from the research shape the plot) and a first person story of someone living through the unit 3 history set. Grade 3 used dialogue, description and time words; grade 4 adds orienting the reader, sensory detail and varied transitions. Limit: pacing as a named technique is grade 5 (W.5.3b).

words: task; purpose; audience; clear; coherent; short write; draft
notes: Produce clear and coherent writing whose development and organization fit task, purpose and audience (W.4.4), and write routinely, daily short responses and longer pieces over days (W.4.10). Introduces the rhetorical-situation model in its simple form: who is this for, what must it do, what form fits. Practised in the daily written exit answer on the day's text and in each unit's pieces; the year's writing keeps the rubric's grades 3 to 5 shares (about 30 opinion, 35 informative, 35 narrative). Grade 3 fitted task and purpose with adult guidance; grade 4 adds audience and drops the guidance clause, so the student judges fit. Limit: the three types; adapting to many contexts is grade 5 and beyond.

words: plan; draft; revise; edit; feedback; publish; type; one page; collaborate
notes: Plan, revise and edit with guidance from peers and adults (W.4.5), and use technology, including the internet, to produce and publish writing and work with others, typing at least one page in a single sitting (W.4.6). Each unit takes a piece through the whole process with a model piece, a peer critique against one look-for, teacher feedback and a published product (the unit 1 poem and talk, the unit 2 adventure story, the unit 4 press release). Grade 3 began keyboarding with no length; grade 4 sets one typed page in a sitting and adds the internet for publishing. Teacher note: rooms without devices handwrite, and the one-page typing goal moves to the home or library session.

words: research; aspect; investigate; notes; category; source; list of sources; relevant
cross_subject: science:4-LS1-1 (research on how animal structures protect them)
notes: Conduct short research projects that investigate different aspects of a topic (W.4.7): gather relevant information from experience and from print and digital sources, take notes, sort it into categories the student makes, and provide a list of sources (W.4.8). Introduces the citation model in its first form: title, author and where it was found. Practised in unit 2 (one animal's body, habitat, predators and defenses, from a research notebook) and unit 4 (how students around the world have made a difference). Grade 3 took brief notes into provided categories from given sources; grade 4 investigates several aspects, makes the categories and lists sources. Limit: summarizing or paraphrasing in notes is grade 5.

words: role; facilitator; clarify; follow up; link; review; key idea; evidence
notes: Take part in discussions prepared by having read the text (1a), following agreed rules and carrying out assigned roles (1b), posing and answering specific questions to clarify or follow up and linking comments to others' remarks (1c), and reviewing the key ideas before explaining one's own view (1d). Practised in at least two formal text-based discussions a unit; the unit 3 performance is a discussion of the history set from both sides, with evidence. Grade 3 came prepared, followed norms and asked questions to check understanding; grade 4 adds roles, follow-up questions and reviewing key ideas. Limit: elaborating on others' remarks and drawing conclusions is grade 5.

words: present; organize; main idea; theme; fact; detail; visual; audio; pace
notes: Report on a topic or text, tell a story or recount an experience in an organized way, with facts and descriptive details that support main ideas or themes, speaking clearly at an understandable pace (SL.4.4), and add audio and visual displays where they strengthen the main ideas or themes (SL.4.5). Practised in the unit 1 poetry presentation (a student reads an original poem aloud and explains what inspired it, with a visual) and unit 4 announcements. Grade 3 reported with facts and details at an understandable pace; grade 4 organizes the talk around a main idea or theme and adds media for a purpose. Limit: presenting an opinion with logically sequenced ideas is grade 5.

words: formal; informal; precise; punctuation; effect; audience; situation
notes: Tell contexts that call for formal English (presenting ideas) from those where informal talk fits (small-group discussion) and use formal English when the task needs it (SL.4.6, L.4.3c). L.4.3 adds choosing words and phrases to convey ideas precisely (3a) and choosing punctuation for effect (3b), taught in the revision step of each process piece. Practised on the unit 1 poem (punctuation for effect) and the unit 4 press release against a note to a classmate. Grade 3 noticed differences between spoken and written English; grade 4 chooses register by context. Limit: two registers; adapting speech to many contexts is grade 5 (SL.5.6).

words: relative pronoun; who; which; that; progressive; modal; can; may; must; preposition; fragment; run-on
notes: Grammar taught on sentences from the anchor texts and students' drafts: relative pronouns and adverbs (1a), progressive tenses (1b), modal auxiliaries for conditions (1c), the usual order of adjectives (1d), prepositional phrases (1e), complete sentences with fragments and run-ons found and fixed (1f), and frequently confused words such as to, too, two and there, their (1g). Sentence combining is the method: relative clauses and prepositional phrases join short sentences. Grade 3 produced simple, compound and complex sentences and simple tenses; grade 4 adds relative clauses, progressive tenses and correcting fragments and run-ons. Limit: perfect tenses and correlative conjunctions are grade 5.

words: capital; comma; quotation marks; direct speech; quotation; compound sentence; spell; reference
notes: Use capitals correctly (2a), commas and quotation marks for direct speech and for quotations from a text (2b), a comma before a coordinating conjunction in a compound sentence (2c), and spell grade-level words correctly, checking references (2d). Spelling follows the grade 4 long-word sequence and the unit word lists. Practised in editing each process piece; quoting a text (2b) is taught with the unit 4 literary essay. Grade 3 punctuated dialogue and spelled words with suffixes; grade 4 adds quotations from a text and the comma in a compound sentence. Limit: introductory-element commas and titles of works are grade 5.

words: quote; quotation; accurately; infer; inference; evidence; explicit
notes: Quote accurately from a text when explaining what it says outright and when drawing inferences (RL.5.1 and RI.5.1, one skill on two kinds of text). W.5.9 is the same work in writing: drawing evidence from texts to support analysis, reflection and research, applying the grade 5 reading standards to literature (9a) and information (9b). Practised daily on every unit's anchors, from the unit 1 novel read whole to the unit 4 disaster texts. Grade 4 referred to details and examples; grade 5 asks for the exact words, correctly copied and punctuated, and for the inference they support (claim, quotation, reasoning). Limit: quoting and explaining; citing several pieces of evidence for an analysis is grade 6.

words: theme; challenge; respond; speaker; reflect; summary; summarize
notes: Determine a theme of a story, drama or poem from details, including how characters respond to challenges or how a poem's speaker reflects on a topic, and summarize the text. Practised on the unit 1 novel read whole (a girl whose family loses its home and must start over as farm workers) and unit 4 poems written after a disaster. Grade 4 found a theme from details and summarized; grade 5 builds the theme from how characters meet challenges and how a speaker reflects. Limit: theme from responses and reflection; how a theme is conveyed through particular details over a whole text is grade 6. Teacher note: the novel deals with a father's death, poverty and forced migration; the teacher previews and gives students room to step back.

words: compare; contrast; character; setting; event; interact; response; specific detail
notes: Compare and contrast two or more characters, settings or events, drawing on specific details, such as how characters interact. Practised on the unit 1 novel (two characters' responses to the same event, written up as a literary essay) and unit 4 stories. Grade 4 described one character, setting or event in depth; grade 5 sets two or more side by side and reads their interactions. Limit: comparing within a story or drama; how a plot unfolds and characters change in response is grade 6.

words: figurative; metaphor; simile; idiom; proverb; synonym; antonym; homograph; interpret
notes: Work out what words and phrases mean in a literary text, including metaphors and similes (RL.5.4). L.5.5 adds interpreting figurative language in context (5a), common idioms, adages and proverbs (5b), and using synonyms, antonyms and homographs to understand each word better (5c). Practised on the unit 1 novel (its metaphors for growing and the land), unit 2 rainforest narratives rich in figurative description, and unit 4 poems. Grade 4 explained simple similes and metaphors; grade 5 interprets figurative language in a passage and says what it adds. Limit: figurative meaning; connotation and the effect of word choice on tone is grade 6.

words: structure; chapter; scene; stanza; fits together; overall; turning point; resolution
notes: Explain how a series of chapters, scenes or stanzas fits together to give the overall structure of a story, drama or poem. Practised on the unit 1 novel read whole (its chapters named for harvests, mapped on the narrative arc) and a unit 4 poem in stanzas. Grade 4 named the elements of poems and drama; grade 3 said how each part builds; grade 5 explains how all the parts make one structure. Limit: how the parts fit; how a single sentence, chapter or scene fits and adds to theme, setting or plot is grade 6.

words: narrator; speaker; point of view; influence; describe; dialect; register; variety
notes: Describe how a narrator's or speaker's point of view shapes how events are described (RL.5.6). L.5.3b adds comparing the varieties of English used in stories, dramas and poems (dialects and registers) and what they tell about the speaker. Practised on unit 4 poems and stories about disasters told by people who lived through them, and the unit 1 novel's dialogue. Grade 4 compared first and third person narration; grade 5 asks what the teller's position changes in the telling. Limit: the narrator's influence; how an author develops a narrator's point of view is grade 6. L.5.3 itself sits on e5-grammar.

words: visual; multimedia; graphic novel; illustration; tone; mood; beauty; meaning
notes: Analyze how visual and multimedia elements add to the meaning, tone or beauty of a text: a graphic novel, a multimedia version of a story, an illustrated folktale or poem. Practised on the unit 4 illustrated story of a boy trapped after an earthquake who survives by imagining, and short videos of poems. Grade 4 matched a story or play to a visual or oral version; grade 5 analyzes what the visual elements contribute. Limit: contribution to meaning, tone, beauty; comparing reading a text with hearing or seeing it is grade 6. Teacher note: disaster stories may touch students who have lived through one; preview and offer a different reading.

words: genre; mystery; adventure; realistic fiction; compare; approach; theme; topic
notes: Compare and contrast stories in the same genre (mysteries, adventure stories) on how they approach similar themes and topics. Practised on two adventure or survival stories in unit 2 (rainforest) or unit 4 (disaster), each 1,500 to 4,000 words, with independent reading in one genre. Grade 4 compared traditional tales across cultures; grade 5 holds the genre fixed and compares approaches. Limit: stories in one genre; comparing texts in different forms or genres is grade 6 (RL.6.9).

words: novel; article; biography; independent reading; log; band; high end
notes: Read stories, plays, poems and information texts at the high end of the grades 4 to 5 band (measure about 740 to 1010) independently and proficiently by year end. RL.5.10 and RI.5.10 are one demand on two kinds of text. Practised through the year's anchors (about half literary, half informational), at least two long texts read whole (the unit 1 novel and the unit 3 biography), and a daily independent reading block with a log and conference. Grade 4 read the band proficiently with scaffolding at the high end; grade 5 reaches the high end alone. Limit: the grades 4 to 5 band; the 6 to 8 band begins in grade 6.

words: main idea; key detail; summary; summarize; several; support
cross_subject: science:5-LS2-1 (main ideas of a text on how matter moves in an ecosystem)
notes: Determine two or more main ideas of a text, explain how key details support each, and summarize (RI.5.2). SL.5.2 adds summarizing a written text read aloud or information in video, charts or talk. Practised on unit 1 articles of a human rights declaration and short commentaries, unit 2 rainforest texts (1,000 to 2,000 words, several sections) and the unit 3 biography. Grade 4 found one main idea and summarized; grade 5 finds several in one text and summarizes a read-aloud, not only paraphrases it. Limit: main ideas and summary; a central idea conveyed through particular details is grade 6.

words: relationship; interaction; individual; event; idea; concept; led to; influenced
cross_subject: science:5-LS2-1 (interactions among living things in an ecosystem)
notes: Explain the relationships or interactions between two or more individuals, events, ideas or concepts in a history, science or technical text, from specific information. Practised on unit 2 rainforest texts (how plants, animals and people depend on each other) and the unit 3 biography (how one athlete, a team owner and fans changed each other). Grade 4 explained one event or idea and why it happened; grade 5 explains how two or more interact. Limit: interactions shown in the text; how a key individual or event is introduced and elaborated is grade 6.

words: structure; chronology; comparison; cause and effect; problem and solution; compare; two texts
cross_subject: social-studies:ss5-civil-rights-movements (a story of change told as a timeline and as a problem and solution)
notes: Compare and contrast the overall structure of events, ideas or information in two or more texts (chronology, comparison, cause and effect, problem and solution). Practised on unit 2 rainforest texts (a scientist's chronology against a problem and solution article on deforestation) and unit 3 texts on athletes. Grade 4 named the structure of one text; grade 5 compares structures across texts and says what each lets the author do. Limit: comparing structures; how one sentence, paragraph or section fits a whole is grade 6.

words: account; point of view; similar; different; source; witness; perspective
cross_subject: social-studies:ss5-sourcing-corroboration (checking accounts against each other)
notes: Analyze several accounts of the same event or topic, noting important similarities and differences in the points of view they represent. Practised on unit 3 accounts of an athlete breaking a barrier (a newspaper of the time, a teammate's memory, the athlete's own words) and unit 4 accounts of one disaster. Grade 4 compared one firsthand and one secondhand account; grade 5 analyzes several and names the point of view each represents. Limit: points of view in accounts; how an author's point of view is conveyed is grade 6. Teacher note: accounts of racism in sport use the words of their time; the teacher previews and frames them.

words: source; print; digital; locate; search; key word; efficient; reliable
cross_subject: social-studies:ss5-civil-rights-research (finding answers in several sources)
notes: Draw on several print and digital sources to find an answer to a question or solve a problem quickly. Practised in unit 2 web research on ways to help the rainforest and unit 4 research on supplies for an emergency kit, on teacher-chosen sources first and then a supervised search. Grade 4 interpreted charts, graphs and timelines inside one text and gathered sources for research; grade 5 moves across several sources at speed and must judge where to look. Limit: locating answers; judging a source's credibility in depth is grade 6 and beyond. Teacher note: open searching is supervised.

words: point; claim; reason; evidence; supports; which; speaker
cross_subject: science:5-PS2-1 (supporting an argument with evidence)
notes: Explain how an author uses reasons and evidence to support particular points, identifying which reasons and evidence support which point (RI.5.8); summarize a speaker's points and explain how each claim is supported (SL.5.3). Introduces the argument-map model: each point with the reasons and evidence hung under it. Practised on unit 3 texts arguing what made an athlete a leader of change and unit 4 texts on the most important preparations. Grade 4 explained how reasons and evidence support points; grade 5 matches each reason to its point, so a text with several points is mapped. Limit: mapping support; judging whether the evidence is sufficient is grade 6 (RI.6.8).

words: integrate; several; sources; synthesize; knowledgeably; compare
notes: Integrate information from several texts on the same topic in order to write or speak about it knowledgeably. Practised in unit 3 (several short biographies of athletes who led change, joined in a compare and contrast essay and a presentation) and unit 4 (texts on one kind of disaster). Grade 4 joined two texts; grade 5 joins several, keeping track of which idea came from which source. Limit: integration on one topic; comparing how two authors present the same events is grade 6 (RI.6.9).

words: biodiversity; canopy; species; ecosystem; barrier; segregation; preparedness; however; although; moreover
cross_subject: science:5-LS2-1 (words for ecosystems and food webs)
notes: Learn and use the general academic and domain words of the grade 5 topics: working out their meaning in a text on a grade 5 topic (RI.5.4) and using them accurately (L.5.6), including words that signal contrast, addition and other logical relationships (however, although, nevertheless, similarly, moreover, in addition). One word list per unit, words met before, during and after reading and again later. Grade 4 added precise action and feeling words and topic-basic words; grade 5 adds the connecting words that carry an argument or explanation. Limit: grade 5 topics.

words: context; cause; comparison; root; affix; photosynthesis; dictionary; thesaurus; pronunciation
notes: Choose a strategy for an unknown or multiple-meaning word: context such as cause and effect or comparison in the text (4a), Greek and Latin affixes and roots (photograph, photosynthesis, 4b), and reference works in print and online for pronunciation and precise meaning (4c). Practised on words the unit texts supply (rainforest science words for roots, human rights articles for context). Grade 4 used definition, example and restatement clues and the first Greek and Latin parts; grade 5 reads relationship clues across a sentence or two and more roots. Limit: grade 5 roots; the part of speech and word position as clues are grade 6.

words: syllable; root; prefix; suffix; stress; schwa; Greek; Latin; multisyllabic
notes: A taught sequence for reading unfamiliar multisyllabic words in and out of context with all letter-sound, syllable and morphology knowledge (3a): four- and five-syllable words, suffixes that change stress and spelling (-ity, -ian, -ial), and the Greek and Latin roots of the year's science and history words (bio, geo, struct, dict, spect). Daily short lessons, then the patterns in sentences and the anchor passages, with checks and next steps. Grade 4 and grade 5 share the wording; grade 5's demand rises in the words themselves (longer, more Greek and Latin, more stress shifts) and in the texts they appear in. The last year of foundational standards: grade 6 carries word parts into vocabulary (L.6.4b).

words: fluency; accuracy; rate; expression; phrasing; reread; self-correct; monologue
notes: Read grade-level prose and poetry aloud with accuracy, a natural rate and expression on successive readings (4b), with purpose and understanding (4a), using context to confirm or fix word recognition (4c). Practised on partner rereading of anchor passages, the unit 1 monologue performed from the novel, and unit 4 poems read aloud. A one-minute oral reading check three times a year with the teacher holding the watch. Same wording as grade 4; the demand rises with the texts (high end of the grades 4 to 5 band) and with performance for an audience. Limit: the last year RF applies; grade 6 keeps a fluency opener without a standard.

words: opinion; reason; logically; fact; detail; consequently; specifically; conclusion
cross_subject: science:5-LS1-1 (an argument supported by evidence)
notes: Write opinion pieces that introduce the topic or text clearly, state the opinion and group ideas logically (1a), give logically ordered reasons supported by facts and details (1b), link opinion and reasons with words, phrases and clauses (consequently, specifically) (1c), and conclude (1d). Practised on the unit 3 essay on which factors most mattered to an athlete's success, planned on an argument map, and the unit 4 essay on the most important items in an emergency kit. Grade 4 backed reasons with facts and details; grade 5 orders the reasons logically and links with clauses. Limit: opinion; a claim answered against an opposing claim is grade 6 argument (W.6.1).

words: observation; focus; logically; heading; quotation; in contrast; especially; precise; conclusion
notes: Write informative text that introduces a topic clearly with a general observation and focus and groups information logically, with headings and media where useful (2a), develops it with facts, definitions, concrete details, quotations and examples (2b), links ideas within and across categories with words, phrases and clauses (in contrast, especially) (2c), uses precise and domain words (2d) and concludes (2e). Practised on the unit 1 literary essay comparing two characters, unit 2 essay on an author's sensory language, and unit 3 essay comparing athletes. Grade 4 grouped information in paragraphs and sections; grade 5 adds a focus statement and links across categories. Limit: a thesis organized by a named structure is grade 6.

words: orient; narrator; dialogue; description; pacing; transition; clause; sensory; conclusion
notes: Write narratives that orient the reader (3a), use narrative techniques such as dialogue, description and pacing (3b), manage sequence with a variety of transitional words, phrases and clauses (3c), use concrete and sensory detail (3d) and conclude from the events (3e). Practised on a unit 1 monologue in a character's voice and a unit 2 first person story set in the rainforest canopy, with facts from the reading. Grade 4 used dialogue, description and sensory detail; grade 5 adds pacing (where to slow down, where to skip) and transition clauses. Limit: grade 6 adds point of view and relevant descriptive detail across a whole narrative.

words: task; purpose; audience; clear; coherent; short write; extended
notes: Produce clear and coherent writing fitted to task, purpose and audience (W.5.4), and write routinely, daily short responses and longer pieces over days (W.5.10). Practised in the daily written answer on the day's text and each unit's pieces; the year keeps the rubric's grades 3 to 5 shares (about 30 opinion, 35 informative, 35 narrative). Grades 4 and 5 share the wording; grade 5's demand rises through the longer texts written from and the grade 5 type standards, and the student plans fit with less help. Limit: the rhetorical-situation model is used to choose form; analysing it in others' writing is later.

words: plan; draft; revise; edit; rewrite; new approach; publish; type; two pages
notes: Plan, revise, edit, rewrite or try a new approach with guidance from peers and adults (W.5.5), and use technology, including the internet, to produce and publish writing and work with others, typing at least two pages in one sitting (W.5.6). Each unit takes a piece through the process with a model piece, peer critique, teacher feedback and publishing (the literary essay, the rainforest story, the athlete presentation, the preparedness leaflet). Grade 4 planned, revised and edited and typed one page; grade 5 adds rewriting and trying a new approach, and two typed pages. Teacher note: rooms without devices handwrite, and the typing goal moves to the home or library session.

words: research; several sources; investigate; summarize; paraphrase; notes; list of sources
cross_subject: science:5-ESS3-1 (finding out how communities protect resources)
notes: Conduct short research projects that use several sources to investigate different aspects of a topic (W.5.7); gather relevant information from experience and print and digital sources, summarize or paraphrase it in notes and finished work, and give a list of sources (W.5.8). Practised in unit 2 (ways people can help the rainforest), unit 3 (athletes who led change) and unit 4 (preparing for a disaster). Grade 4 took notes, sorted them and listed sources; grade 5 requires several sources and summarizing or paraphrasing in notes, the first guard against copying. Limit: a list of sources in a simple form; a standard citation format is grade 6 (W.6.8).

words: prepare; role; elaborate; build on; question; conclusion; key idea; evidence
notes: Take part in discussions prepared by having read the text (1a), following rules and carrying out roles (1b), posing and answering specific questions with comments that elaborate on others' remarks (1c), and reviewing key ideas and drawing conclusions from the discussion (1d). Practised in at least two formal text-based discussions a unit, beginning with the unit 1 discussion of threats to human rights in the novel. Grade 4 linked comments and reviewed key ideas; grade 5 elaborates on others' remarks and draws a conclusion from the talk. Limit: grade 6 adds probing questions and paraphrasing others' views.

words: report; present; opinion; sequence; logically; multimedia; formal; adapt
notes: Report on a topic or text or present an opinion, sequencing ideas logically with facts and descriptive details that support main ideas or themes, speaking clearly at an understandable pace (SL.5.4); include multimedia and visual displays where they strengthen the main ideas (SL.5.5); adapt speech to contexts and tasks, using formal English when appropriate (SL.5.6). Practised on the unit 3 multimedia presentation on leaders of change and the unit 4 recorded announcement on staying safe. Grade 4 organized a report and told formal from informal; grade 5 adds presenting an opinion and adapting speech to many contexts. Limit: claims with pertinent evidence in a presentation is grade 6.

words: conjunction; preposition; interjection; perfect tense; had; have; will have; either; neither; shift; expand; combine; reduce
notes: Grammar taught on sentences from the anchor texts and students' drafts: what conjunctions, prepositions and interjections do in a sentence (1a), perfect tenses (1b), verb tense to show time, sequence, state and condition (1c), finding and fixing shifts in tense (1d), correlative conjunctions (1e). L.5.3 adds expanding, combining and reducing sentences for meaning, interest and style (3a), the sentence-combining method by name; its second part, varieties of English (3b), sits on e5-narrator-influence. Grade 4 used relative clauses and progressive tenses and fixed fragments; grade 5 adds perfect tenses and tense shifts. Limit: pronoun case and intensive pronouns are grade 6.

words: comma; series; introductory; yes; no; direct address; tag question; title; italics; underline; spell
notes: Use punctuation to separate items in a series (2a), a comma after an introductory element (2b), commas to set off yes and no, a tag question and direct address (2c), underlining, quotation marks or italics for titles of works (2d), and spell grade-level words correctly with references (2e). Spelling follows the grade 5 long-word sequence and the unit word lists. Practised in editing each process piece and in the unit 4 recorded announcement script. Grade 4 used commas in compound sentences and quotations; grade 5 adds the introductory comma, direct address and titles. Limit: commas for nonrestrictive elements are grade 6.
